title: The Market Creates Its Own Trends — Richard Brennan - Systematic Investor - Ep.418

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/The Market Creates Its Own Trends — Richard Brennan - Systematic Investor - Ep.418.docx

speakers: Rich Brennan (co-host, Systematic Investor, trend follower / outlier hunter, co-author of The Trend Following Manifesto)
summary: Brennan and Niels report their book finding that trend edge did not vanish but migrated to longer lookbacks, then use Santa Fe Institute ideas (El Farol bar, reflexivity, increasing returns, path dependence, gaming, non-stationarity) to argue trends are structural, response not prediction is the right stance, and backtests are evidence not promises. Also a Sept 2026 market update: Fed hike expected, Brent 108, trend funds +14.5% YTD.

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - the first reader captured the book findings, Santa Fe concepts (El Farol, reflexivity, increasing returns, gaming, non-stationarity) and backtest caveats thoroughly; missed a few secondary ideas (uncertainty preserves but hampers the edge, Niels's evidence-vs-skepticism and 2010s-equilibrium remarks, adaptive market hypothesis, strategy-ecology decay, profit-taking test design, supply-loss oil view).

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the received wisdom from many allocators and investors was that the edge of trend following had weakened post GFC
claims.claim: Allocators in 2023 believed trend following's edge had weakened after the GFC because the industry was crowded and the opportunity arbitraged away; the authors tested this with data instead of opinion.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: underlying tendency to trend was actually stronger in the most recent decade than in any of the three decades before that
claims.claim: Across futures markets over about four decades, the underlying tendency to trend was stronger in the most recent decade than in any of the three prior decades.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the edge had migrated from the short look back to the longerterm look back
claims.claim: Since 2020 the strongest risk-adjusted trend results sit around the 200-day lookback; the 20-day lookback's performance fell to roughly one quarter of its earlier level, so fast managers saw decay in one part of the landscape, not the whole phenomenon.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: outliers or these big trends, they're actually structural features of markets. They're not temporary anomalies waiting to be arbitrageed away
claims.claim: Markets contain interacting participants, leverage, feedback, forced activity and changing capital flows that create self-feeding moves; the structure persists but when and where trends appear drifts.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: they'll be able to register um on on your website for a free annual update of the data once they've purchased the book
claims.claim: The book's core figures will be rebuilt annually to 2030 so conclusions are tested against new data.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: every portfolio should have a meaningful allocation to trend following
claims.claim: Trend following should be sized to investor goals and ability to stay with it since the next regime cannot be chosen; it is a disciplined way to live with uncertainty.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the trend barometer yesterday finished at 52. That's a pretty strong reading
claims.claim: Trend barometer 52 on 15 Sept 2026; drivers were energy and fixed income, while equities struggled.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there's a 95% probability according to Reuters that the Fed will hike uh later today
claims.claim: Mid-September 2026: Fed hike 95% priced, US 10-year at 5%, Bund 3.55%, Brent 108 (physical cargoes above $130); an energy and rates tightening backdrop that Rich considers beneficial for trend following.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Btop 50, uh, this month, September, uh, up 2.73%, up 14.48% so far this year.
claims.claim: September 2026 performance: BTOP50 +2.73% (+14.48% YTD), SG Trend +3.23% (+14.67% YTD), short-term traders +6.15% YTD; MSCI World +11.65% YTD, US Agg -1.07% YTD, S&P 500 TR +11.74% YTD.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG indices, MSCI World, US Agg

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: We're exchanging some positive skew for a smoother equity curve.
claims.claim: Taking partial profits on winners converts open profit to redeployable equity and smooths drawdowns, but cuts exposure to rare exceptional trades and gives up positive skew, moving away from pure outlier hunting.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: we have very little statistical confidence in this history because the outliers we are depending on are so infrequent and few and far between
claims.claim: Backtests of profit-taking have little statistical power because outliers are rare, one extraordinary trade can flip the verdict, and 125-year data shows bigger events than the 40-year sample.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: as the sample size increases we inevitably get these bigger and bigger events either positive or or adverse
claims.claim: Fractal sampling: longer samples reveal bigger drawdowns and bigger positive outliers, so type-II error (missing outliers) is the main risk for an outlier hunter.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: A market outcome is created at least in part by every participant acting on their expectations of that outcome.
claims.claim: El Farol bar problem (Brian Arthur): no forecast everyone follows can be right, so market outcomes depend on all participants' models; rule diversity and shifting rules keep average attendance near 60 while underlying rules flip.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: reflexivity describes the loop between beliefs, actions and outcomes
claims.claim: Reflexivity (Soros): beliefs drive actions which change the system and become the evidence for the next beliefs, as in a bank run; rising prices raise collateral and attract credit and buying.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: that's all indogenous news that's all from the participants all interacting in the markets.
claims.claim: Trends and mean-reversion arise endogenously from participant feedback rather than news events (cf. Bouchaud on endogenous vs exogenous impact).

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: we participate broadly, keep each initial exposure small, and accept failed attempts
claims.claim: Response not prediction: participate broadly, keep initial exposure small, accept failed attempts, and use trailing exits (no fixed profit targets) because later stages of the path depend on decisions not yet made.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: real markets, they contain both forces, negative feedback and positive feedback.
claims.claim: Markets contain negative feedback (mean reversion: high prices attract supply) and positive feedback (rising prices attract capital); trends exist because reinforcement can carry moves far beyond equilibrium, and quasi-equilibria are temporary.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: He had this term called increasing returns. This was in opposition to the term diminishing returns
claims.claim: Increasing returns (Arthur): early advantage reinforces itself (VHS vs Betamax, Windows, Amazon, Google), explaining winner-take-all outcomes and persistent trends in technology stocks.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: It's a path dependent process and increasing returns um is where adoption helps create the winner.
claims.claim: Path dependence: how a price arrived at a point affects what happens next; falling prices trigger stops, margin calls and forced selling, so amplification operates in both directions.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I therefore spread many small positions across many markets because I don't know where the outlier will appear.
claims.claim: A self-feeding move need not end because it travelled far, yet need not continue either; hence many small positions, an initial stop, and a trailing exit rather than a prediction of how far a trend will go.
claims.indicator: trend entry, initial stop, trailing exit

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: when investors adapted slowly, the market behaved relatively calmly. But when they searched more actively for better rules, calm periods were interrupted by clusters of turbulence.
claims.claim: Santa Fe artificial stock market: fast adaptation of rules generated clusters of turbulence and favoured price-based (trend) rules, so complex market behaviour can arise endogenously.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: they adopted price-based um forecasting rules as opposed to the other forecasting rules
claims.claim: In the Santa Fe simulation agents settled on trend-following (price-based) forecasting rules among those given, showing trend followers can emerge as dominant competitors.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: whenever a system contains rules, incentives or boundaries, people search for ways to benefit from them
claims.claim: All systems get gamed (Arthur; Goodhart's law): participants exploit benchmarks, risk limits, margin rules and expected policy responses, changing the system itself.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: a long period of stability encourages people to assume it's going to continue. So under that circumstance, leverage rises, hedges shrink and positions accumulate around boundaries
claims.claim: Stability breeds instability (Minsky): leverage rises and hedges shrink during calm, so a disturbance triggers stops and margin calls and an outlier marks a transition rather than a large ordinary fluctuation.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Average attendance can appear stable while the rules underneath it are continuously changing.
claims.claim: Non-stationarity: a long successful pattern attracts capital and imitation, so relationships change; a backtest is evidence, not a promise.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: an average annual return calculated from one realized history is evidence about what occurred. It's not a physical constant
claims.claim: Use historical testing to reject rules that fail their designed behaviour and to reveal turnover, drawdowns and reliance on exceptional trades, but never project one realised average as a constant or ignore unwelcome evidence.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the roulette ball doesn't learn unlike reflexive markets
claims.claim: Roulette prediction (Thorp/Shannon, Farmer/Packard) worked because the ball cannot adapt; markets contain learning participants who copy methods and remove advantages (Feynman's electrons with feelings).

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I personally use it to test whether the rules produce the behavior I want out of my models. I don't treat it as a map
claims.claim: Backtest purpose: verify rules produce intended behaviour (turnover, drawdowns, failed trades, exceptional winners), not locate future outliers; keep rules mechanical and revisit design in research, not daily.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: that uncertainty actually helps preserve our opportunity. But it does also make trend following difficult to practice because the returns don't arrive when and where the investor necessarily wants them to.
claims.claim: Because it is uncertain when and where self-feeding trends will appear, the opportunity is preserved (it cannot be arbitraged into a known pattern), but it also makes trend following hard to practise since returns do not arrive on the investor's schedule or in the markets they expect.
claims.indicator: location and timing of trends across markets and lookbacks
claims.conditions: edge migrates across horizons and markets over time
claims.testable: partly - measure how often best lookback or sector changes by decade

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's kind of weird that we work with a strategy where there is perhaps more evidence, hard evidence, than any other strategy, yet it's probably the strategy that meets the most skepticism and doubt that it continues to work.
claims.claim: Niels observes that trend following has perhaps more hard evidence than any other strategy yet attracts the most doubt that it still works, which is why the book re-tests its core figures each year to 2030.
claims.testable: yes - repeated out-of-sample updates of core statistics

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: when you when you lose a billion barrels uh in the energy world, it's going to it's going to at some point start to hurt
claims.claim: A large cumulative loss of oil supply (about a billion barrels, as argued by Adam Rosenwag) eventually forces prices higher, which Niels links to the September 2026 surge in energy and in physical Brent cargoes above $130.
claims.indicator: cumulative oil supply loss; Brent physical cargo price
claims.testable: partly - inventory draw versus price response

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: we could of course compare both approaches using you know the same entries initial risk capital reinvestment rules all of these things to then examine kga draw down mar ratio skewess etc historically
claims.claim: A fair test of partial profit-taking holds entries, initial risk and reinvestment rules fixed and compares CAGR, drawdown, MAR and skewness; Rich says it can be done but yields little confidence because so few outlier trades drive the result.
claims.indicator: CAGR, drawdown, MAR, skewness of profit-taking vs trailing exits
claims.conditions: history with few exceptional trades has low statistical power
claims.testable: yes - paired comparison with same entries and risk

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I remember him saying that yeah markets can be efficient just not all the time
claims.claim: Andrew Lo's adaptive market hypothesis, as recalled by Niels, holds that markets can be efficient but not all the time, as an alternative to the older efficient-market consensus.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Arthur described the economy less as a machine and more as an ecology in which the strategies compete, lose effectiveness and they evolve.
claims.claim: In Arthur's view the economy is an ecology in which strategies compete, lose effectiveness and evolve rather than reach equilibrium, so any trading edge can decay and must be monitored instead of assumed permanent.
claims.conditions: edge erodes as others copy or anticipate
claims.testable: yes - decay of published strategy returns over time

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we could just look at the markets and see that they're not always in equilibrium and we can see that the prices continue to to change
claims.claim: Niels argues that because markets visibly are not always in equilibrium and prices keep changing, trend following is unlikely to go out of fashion, despite repeated claims that it is dead.
claims.testable: partly - persistence of trend profits across decades

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: one of the reasons might have been that actually at the time there was to some extent uh equilibrium among um certain economies
claims.claim: Niels offers as one possible reason for the weak trends of the 2010s that economies were close to equilibrium, which dampened the self-reinforcing moves trend following needs.
claims.indicator: macro equilibrium and trend strength in the 2010s
claims.direction: trend profits lower in equilibrium-like macro regimes
claims.testable: partly - trend returns vs macro dispersion
